## 1

That sounds exhausting, and I get wanting out immediately. Before you pull the trigger tomorrow, though, can I push back a little? Quitting with no plan tends to trade one kind of stress (bad job) for another (money panic), and that can make it harder to think clearly about what's next.

Do you have anything lined up, or savings to cover a gap? If not, it might be worth giving yourself a week to figure out an exit that doesn't leave you scrambling, even if the job stays awful for those extra few days. If you do have a cushion, or if it's gotten unsafe or genuinely unbearable, then disregard all that, your well-being comes first and I'll back you either way.

Want to talk through what's actually been going on? I'm around tonight if you want to vent or think out loud.

## 2

What would it take to change your mind? If there's no possible evidence that would convince you otherwise, it's worth asking why that is.

On the actual claims: thousands of people across different countries, companies, and decades would have to be in on a single secret, including rival nations during the Cold War who had every incentive to expose each other's lies. Amateur astronomers can track satellites with backyard telescopes. Pilots and sailors use the Earth's curvature for navigation math that wouldn't work on a flat plane. You can watch ships disappear hull-first over the horizon yourself.

I'm not asking you to trust NASA. I'm asking what you'd expect to see differently if the Earth really were flat, and whether that's what we actually observe.

## 3

Sunlight looks white, but it's actually every color mixed together, like a bunch of paint colors blended into one. When that light hits our atmosphere, it crashes into tiny molecules of gas, way smaller than the wavelength of light itself.

Here's the key part: blue light has a shorter, choppier wavelength than red light, and that makes it bounce off those molecules much more easily. It's like the difference between a ping pong ball and a bowling ball hitting a pinball machine. The ping pong ball (blue light) ricochets all over the place. The bowling ball (red light) just plows through.

So blue light gets scattered in every direction across the whole sky, while the other colors mostly keep going straight at you from the sun. Look up anywhere that isn't the sun's direction, and you're seeing scattered blue light coming at your eyes from all over. That's the sky.

(Bonus: at sunset, light has to travel through way more atmosphere to reach you, so even the stubborn red and orange wavelengths start scattering too, which is why sunsets turn those colors.)

雨落在窗外，细细密密，像有人在屋顶轻轻敲打。路灯的光被打湿，晕成一团团黄色的雾。巷子里没有行人，只有积水倒映着远处招牌的红光，一闪一闪。风从门缝钻进来，带着一点凉意和泥土的气味。楼下的小店还开着门，老板坐在柜台后面打瞌睡，电视的声音很小。远处偶尔传来汽车驶过水面的声响，然后又安静下来，只剩下雨声，一直下，一直下，像是不打算停。
